title: Certainty and Possibility
overview: Level 1 used modals to talk about rules — what you have to do, what you must not do. This unit uses the same words for something completely different: working out what is true. Must, might and can't stop being about obligation and start being about deduction, and the same three words then reach backwards to talk about what should have happened. It ends with an investigation report where every conclusion is a deduction.
learningPath: Read and listen to the Lesson. There are three patterns.
Open Patterns. Card 1 uses words you know for a job you have not seen them do.
Learn the words. Twenty-nine, in five groups.
Read the three texts aloud. The third is an investigation report and its conclusions.
Do the Practice. Practice 2 is where should have and must have get confused.
Record yourself deducing what happened from six sets of evidence.
Take the quiz, then update My progress.
lectureScript:
In Level 1 you learned must and must not for rules. You must wear safety shoes. You must not enter this area. That is obligation, and it is Unit 17 of Level 1.
This unit uses the same words for something else entirely, and that surprises people, so let me be direct about it. Must, might and can't have a second job, and it is deduction — working out what is true from evidence.
Here is the whole system, and it is a scale of certainty.
Must be — you are almost certain it is true. The lights are on, so somebody must be in.
Might be, may be, could be — it is possible. She might be in the other bay.
Can't be — you are almost certain it is not true. He can't be in the office; I just saw him leave.
Three positions on one scale: almost certainly yes, possibly, almost certainly no.
And here is the thing that catches everybody. The opposite of must be is not mustn't be. It is can't be.
Mustn't is obligation — it means forbidden, from Level 1 Unit 17. It has nothing to do with deduction.
So: he must be in. He can't be in. Those are the two ends. He mustn't be in would mean he is forbidden to be there, which is a different sentence about a different subject.
That is the single most useful thing on this card, and it is worth saying to yourself a few times.
One more point about the form. These modals are followed by be, or by a plain verb.
He must be tired. She might know. It can't be right.
And for something happening now, use be plus the -ing form. He must be waiting. She might be working late.
Second pattern: past modals. This is the same three words reaching backwards.
Must have plus the past participle — you are almost certain about something in the past. The door was open, so somebody must have been in.
Might have, may have, could have — it was possible. She might have forgotten.
Can't have — you are almost certain it did not happen. He can't have seen it; he wasn't there.
So the whole scale moves back in time by adding have and the participle. Nothing else changes.
And then there are two more that only exist in the past, and they are the ones people actually want.
Should have — the right thing to do, and it did not happen. I should have asked. Somebody should have checked it.
That carries regret or criticism. It is how English says something went wrong without saying whose fault it was, and it is extremely common.
Could have — it was possible and it did not happen. It could have been much worse. I could have said something and I did not.
Now the confusion, and it is the main thing this unit has to fix.
Should have and must have are not the same, and learners mix them constantly.
Somebody must have checked it means: I am almost certain somebody did.
Somebody should have checked it means: nobody did, and that was wrong.
Those describe opposite situations. One says it happened; the other says it did not.
The test: must have is a deduction about what did happen. Should have is a judgement about what did not.
And one more that is worth having: needn't have. I needn't have worried — I did worry, and it turned out to be unnecessary. That is different again from didn't need to, which means it was unnecessary and you may not have done it at all.
Third pattern: could and might for possibility, and the difference between them and the deduction use.
When you say she might be in the other bay, you are deducing.
When you say we could try restarting it, you are not deducing anything — you are raising an option.
Same word, two jobs, and English separates them by what follows.
Could for a suggestion is very common and very useful, because it puts an idea on the table without pushing it. We could postpone it. You could ask her directly. Compare we should postpone it, which is advice, and we must postpone it, which is a decision.
So the three make a scale of pressure: could is an option, should is advice, must is a decision. Choosing the wrong one is not a grammar error and it changes how much you are asking of somebody.
And one last thing about hedging. Might and could soften a claim without weakening it, exactly like the hedges in Unit 7. There might be a problem with the seal is a real statement. It leaves room to be wrong, which is what you want when you are deducing rather than reporting.
Go to Patterns.

words.meaning: Without doubt.
words.example: It certainly happened after Tuesday.
words.tutor: Say certainly and almost certainly. The second is what a careful report would use.

words.meaning: It is reasonable to assume, though not confirmed.
words.example: Presumably somebody moved it.
practice: Presumably that is why nobody checked.
words.tutor: Presumably marks a deduction rather than a fact. Say it, then say must have.

words.meaning: According to what appears or what has been said.
words.example: Apparently nobody was told.
practice: Apparently it had been like that for days.
words.tutor: Apparently distances you from the claim. Say it, and say who might have told you.

words.meaning: As it appears, though it may not be so.
words.example: Seemingly nothing had been done.
practice: Seemingly straightforward, and it was not.
words.tutor: Seemingly carries a hint that appearances may mislead. Say apparently and seemingly.

words.meaning: According to a claim that has not been proved.
words.example: He allegedly moved the trolley.
practice: The fault was allegedly known about.
words.tutor: Allegedly signals the claim is untested, from Unit 9. Say allegation and allegedly.

words.meaning: According to what is generally believed, often with doubt.
words.example: It was supposedly checked on Monday.
practice: He is supposedly in charge of it.
words.tutor: Supposedly usually implies you doubt it. Say supposedly and presumably.

words.meaning: To work something out from the evidence.
words.example: From the marks we deduced it had been dragged.
practice: What can we deduce from that?
It was deduced rather than observed.
words.starter: From the marks we deduced it had been
words.tutor: Say deduced rather than observed. That distinction runs through the whole unit.

words.meaning: To conclude something from what is said or shown, rather than being told.
words.example: I inferred that nobody had been asked.
practice: What are we meant to infer?
Nothing should be inferred from silence.
It can be inferred but it is not stated.
words.starter: I inferred that nobody had been
words.tutor: Infer is what the reader does; imply is what the writer does. Say both.

words.meaning: To suggest something without stating it.
words.example: The letter implies she was at fault.
practice: I did not mean to imply that.
It implies more than it says.
words.starter: The letter implies she was at
words.tutor: Say the writer implies and the reader infers. They are opposite ends of the same act.

words.meaning: To suppose something is true without proof.
words.example: I presumed somebody had checked it.
practice: It is presumed to be safe.
words.tutor: Say I presumed and I assumed, from Unit 7. They are very close.

words.meaning: To guess about something without enough evidence.
words.example: I would rather not speculate about why.
practice: The report speculates in two places.
It is speculation, not a finding.
words.starter: I would rather not speculate about
words.tutor: Say I would rather not speculate. It is a useful refusal when you do not know.

words.meaning: To decide something is not possible.
words.example: We can rule out the seal, because it was replaced in March.
practice: That rules out the second option.
words.starter: We can rule out the seal, because it was replaced in
words.tutor: Rule out is the phrasal verb version of can't have. Say both about the same evidence.

words.meaning: Understanding of an event only after it has happened.
words.example: With hindsight, somebody should have checked it.
words.starter: With hindsight, somebody should have checked
words.tutor: With hindsight pairs naturally with should have. Say the two together.

words.meaning: A mistake made by not noticing something.
words.example: It was an oversight rather than a decision.
practice: It was nobody's fault — an oversight.
words.starter: It was an oversight rather than a
words.tutor: Oversight means a thing missed, and also means supervision. Say one sentence with each.

words.meaning: A serious and careless mistake.
words.example: It was a blunder, and it was avoidable.
practice: The blunder was in the first paragraph.
One blunder is not a pattern.
words.starter: It was a blunder, and it was
words.tutor: Blunder is much stronger than oversight. Say both about the same mistake.

words.meaning: To form a wrong opinion about something.
words.example: I misjudged how long it would take.
practice: It was misjudged from the start.
words.starter: I misjudged how long it would
words.tutor: Notice mis- from Unit 8. Say misjudge, misunderstand, misquote.

words.meaning: To know or expect that something will happen.
words.example: Nobody could have foreseen it.
practice: The problem was foreseen and ignored.
words.tutor: Nobody could have foreseen it is a past modal defence. Say it, then say it was foreseeable.

words.meaning: To expect something and prepare for it.
words.example: We had not anticipated the delay.
practice: We anticipate a decision by Friday.
Anticipating is not the same as fearing.
words.tutor: Say anticipate and foresee. One involves preparing; one only involves knowing.

words.meaning: Required to explain and answer for something.
words.example: Somebody has to be accountable for the decision.
practice: She is accountable to the board.
words.starter: Somebody has to be accountable for the
words.tutor: Notice accountable for a thing and accountable to a person. Say both.

words.meaning: Failing to take proper care.
words.example: It was careless rather than negligent.
words.tutor: Negligent is a strong and quasi-legal word. Say careless and negligent about the same act.

words.meaning: To show that something was reasonable or right.
words.example: The evidence does not justify that conclusion.
practice: How do you justify the cost?
words.starter: The evidence does not justify that
words.tutor: Say the evidence does not justify. It disagrees with a conclusion without attacking anybody.

words.meaning: To make something less severe.
words.example: Two things mitigate the failure.
practice: The delay was mitigated by the backup.
words.tutor: Say mitigating circumstances. It is the standard phrase in a finding.

words.meaning: To clear somebody of blame.
words.example: The findings exonerate her completely.
practice: Exonerated rather than merely not blamed.
words.tutor: Say exonerate and clear. The first is formal and appears in reports.

words.meaning: Responsibility for something bad.
words.example: The blame was never formally allocated.
words.tutor: Notice the passive in the example. Say who is missing, using Unit 10.

words.meaning: Possible to imagine, though unlikely.
words.example: It is conceivable but I would not expect it.
practice: It is conceivable that nobody noticed.
words.starter: It is conceivable but I would not
words.tutor: Conceivable is weaker than possible. Say conceivable, possible, likely, in order.

words.meaning: Seeming reasonable and believable.
words.example: That is a plausible explanation.
practice: It sounds plausible and it is wrong.
words.tutor: Say plausible does not mean true. It is worth remembering when judging a report.

words.meaning: Able to be done in practice.
words.example: It is feasible but not within the budget.
words.starter: It is feasible but not within the
words.tutor: Say feasible and possible. Feasible means possible in practice.

words.meaning: Very unlikely; or far away.
words.example: The chance of that is remote.
practice: The risk is remote but real.
words.tutor: Say a remote possibility. It concedes that something could happen while dismissing it.

words.meaning: Very small, of a chance.
words.example: The chances are slim.
practice: A slim chance is still a chance.
words.tutor: Say slim and remote about the same chance. They are close in meaning.

readings.title: The Opposite of Must Is Not Mustn't
readings.passage:
In Level 1 Unit 17 you learned must and mustn't for rules. You must wear safety shoes. You mustn't enter this area. That is obligation.
This unit uses the same words for a completely different job: working out what is true.
The lights are on, so somebody must be in.
That is not a rule about anybody. It is a deduction from evidence.
The system is a scale of three.
Must be — you are almost certain it is true.
Might be, may be, could be — it is possible.
Can't be — you are almost certain it is not true.
And here is the point that catches nearly everybody, and it is worth reading twice.
The opposite of must be is not mustn't be. It is can't be.
He must be in. He can't be in. Those are the two ends of the scale.
He mustn't be in means he is forbidden to be there. That is the Level 1 use, it is about rules, and it has nothing to do with deduction.
So the two jobs of must never overlap, even though they use the same word, and the negative is where they separate. Obligation negates with mustn't; deduction negates with can't.
One small thing about form. These modals are followed by be, or by a plain verb.
He must be tired. She might know. It can't be right.
And for something in progress now, use be plus the -ing form. He must be waiting. She might be working late.
One last observation, which is about how English actually sounds. Deduction is where hedging lives most naturally. There might be a problem with the seal is a real claim — it says you think there is one. It also leaves room for you to be wrong, which is exactly what you want when you are reasoning from evidence rather than reporting what you saw.
A report that states every deduction flatly is not more confident. It is less careful, and a reader who notices will trust the rest of it less.

readings.title: Must Have and Should Have Are Opposites
readings.passage:
Add have and a past participle, and the whole scale moves backwards.
The door was open, so somebody must have been in. Almost certainly they were.
She might have forgotten. It was possible.
He can't have seen it; he wasn't there. Almost certainly he did not.
That is the same three positions, reaching into the past, and nothing else changes.
Then there are two forms that exist only in the past, and one of them is the source of the most persistent confusion in this area.
Should have — the right thing to do, and it did not happen.
Could have — it was possible, and it did not happen.
Now the confusion.
Somebody must have checked it.
Somebody should have checked it.
Learners use these interchangeably and they describe opposite situations.
Must have checked it means: I am almost certain somebody did check it. It happened.
Should have checked it means: nobody checked it, and that was wrong. It did not happen.
One is a deduction about what occurred. The other is a judgement about what did not.
The test is short. Must have is about what did happen. Should have is about what did not.
Apply it to any sentence and the choice resolves immediately.
This matters beyond exercises, because should have is how English assigns fault without naming anybody. Somebody should have checked it says a failure occurred and does not say whose. Combine it with the passive from Unit 10 — it should have been checked — and there is no person in the sentence at all.
So when you read an investigation or a decision, the should haves tell you where the writer thinks things went wrong, and the absence of a name after them tells you how far they were prepared to go.
One further form worth having: needn't have. I needn't have worried means I did worry and it turned out to be unnecessary. That is different from I didn't need to worry, which means it was unnecessary and I may never have worried at all.

readings.title: What the Evidence Supports
readings.setting: The conclusions section of a short internal investigation, with the evidence it rests on.
readings.passage:
EVIDENCE

  E1  The seal was replaced on 3 March.
  E2  Water was found inside the unit on
      17 March.
  E3  The maintenance log has no entry
      between 3 and 17 March.
  E4  The unit was moved on 11 March.
  E5  Two staff report hearing a knock
      during the move.

  CONCLUSIONS

  C1  The seal cannot have been the
      original cause, as it was replaced
      two weeks earlier.

  C2  The damage must have occurred
      between 3 and 17 March.

  C3  The unit may have been damaged
      during the move on 11 March. Two
      staff report a knock, though
      neither saw the unit afterwards.

  C4  The fault should have been
      identified at the weekly check.
      No weekly check was recorded.

  C5  It is conceivable that the
      replacement seal was itself
      faulty, though there is no
      evidence for this and the
      supplier has not been contacted.

  C6  Somebody must have known the unit
      had been knocked.

readings.title: Could, Should, Must: Three Amounts of Pressure
readings.passage:
There is a second use of could that has nothing to do with deduction, and it is one of the most useful things in this unit.
We could postpone it.
That is not a guess about what is true. It is an option being put on the table.
Compare the three:
We could postpone it. — an option. No pressure at all.
We should postpone it. — advice. You think it is the right thing.
We must postpone it. — a decision. It is not open to discussion.
Same structure, three completely different amounts of pressure, and choosing the wrong one is not a grammatical error. It changes how much you are asking of the person you are speaking to.
Could is undervalued by learners, and it does something the other two cannot. It lets you introduce an idea without owning it. You could ask her directly puts a suggestion in front of somebody and leaves them entirely free to reject it, which means they can consider it properly rather than defending themselves against it.
This connects directly to Unit 7. Could and might are hedges, and in a disagreement they let you raise an alternative without turning it into a contest.
There might be another way of doing this. We could try it the other way round.
Both of those are real proposals. Neither of them is a challenge.
One caution, and it is the same one as in Unit 7. If everything you say is could, nobody knows what you think. Reserve should for the things you actually recommend and must for the things that are genuinely decided, and could does its work by contrast with them.
And note the past forms, which are where regret lives.
We could have postponed it. — it was possible, and we did not.
We should have postponed it. — it was right, and we did not.
The first is an observation. The second is a criticism, including of yourself.

comprehension.q: What is the opposite of he must be in?
comprehension.a: He can't be in. Not he mustn't be in, which means he is forbidden to be there.
comprehension.why: Obligation negates with mustn't and deduction negates with can't, and this is where the two jobs of must separate.

comprehension.q: What are the three positions on the deduction scale?
comprehension.a: Must be — almost certainly true. Might, may or could be — possible. Can't be — almost certainly not true.
comprehension.why: Seeing it as one scale rather than three separate words is what makes the negative predictable.

comprehension.q: Why does the text say a report that states every deduction flatly is less careful?
comprehension.a: Because deduction is reasoning from evidence rather than reporting what was seen, so it should leave room to be wrong. A reader who notices the missing hedges trusts the rest of the report less.
comprehension.why: It connects hedging to credibility rather than to politeness, which is the argument that persuades people who think hedging is weak.

comprehension.q: What is the difference between somebody must have checked it and somebody should have checked it?
comprehension.a: The first means you are almost certain somebody did check it. The second means nobody did, and that was wrong.
comprehension.why: They describe opposite situations — one says it happened, the other says it did not — and learners use them interchangeably.

comprehension.q: What is the test that separates them?
comprehension.a: Must have is about what did happen. Should have is about what did not.
comprehension.why: It resolves any sentence in one step, without needing to reason about certainty or obligation.

comprehension.q: How does should have combine with the passive from Unit 10?
comprehension.a: It should have been checked has no person in it at all — the should have says a failure occurred and the passive removes whoever failed.
comprehension.why: It shows two units combining to produce agentless blame, which is exactly what investigation documents do.

comprehension.q: What is the difference between could, should and must as suggestions?
comprehension.a: Could is an option with no pressure, should is advice, and must is a decision that is not open to discussion.
comprehension.why: The choice is not a grammar question and it changes how much is being asked of the listener.

comprehension.q: Conclusion C1 uses cannot have been. What does that claim, and does the evidence support it?
comprehension.a: It claims near-certainty that the seal was not the original cause. E1 supports it — the seal was replaced two weeks before the water was found — so the modal matches the evidence.
comprehension.why: It is the strongest form of negative deduction and here it is properly earned, which makes it the benchmark for judging the others.

comprehension.q: Compare C3 and C5. Both are tentative. Are they equally well supported?
comprehension.a: No. C3 says may have been damaged and rests on E4 and E5 — a move on the right date and two people hearing a knock. C5 says it is conceivable and states plainly that there is no evidence at all and the supplier has not been contacted.
comprehension.why: Both are hedged, and one hedge covers a supported possibility while the other covers a pure guess. The strength of the modal is not the same as the strength of the evidence.

comprehension.q: C6 says somebody must have known. Is that the same kind of claim as C2?
comprehension.a: No. C2 deduces a time window from dated evidence. C6 deduces a state of mind from an event, with nothing in the evidence about who was present or what anybody noticed. It is much weaker and it is stated just as strongly.
comprehension.why: This is the one conclusion in the report where the modal outruns the evidence, and spotting it is the point of the whole document.

grammar.title: Modals of deduction
grammar.explanation: Must, might and can't doing a completely different job from Level 1 Unit 17. Not rules — deduction, working out what is true from evidence.
grammar.rule:
A SCALE OF THREE

  MUST BE   almost certainly true
     The lights are on, so somebody
     must be in.

  MIGHT / MAY / COULD BE   possible
     She might be in the other bay.

  CAN'T BE  almost certainly NOT true
     He can't be in; I saw him leave.

THE OPPOSITE OF MUST BE IS CAN'T BE.
  NOT mustn't be.

  he must be in   /  he can't be in
     ^ the two ends of the scale
  he mustn't be in
     ^ FORBIDDEN. Level 1 Unit 17.
     Nothing to do with deduction.

FORM
  modal + BE, or modal + PLAIN VERB
     He must be tired.  She might know.
  happening now: modal + BE + -ING
     He must be waiting.
     She might be working late.

HEDGING IS NORMAL HERE
  you are reasoning, not reporting.
  Leaving room to be wrong is correct.
grammar.workedExample:
You arrive at the office and the lights are on.
1. What are you doing — reporting, or working something out? Working it out. There is nobody in sight.
2. How certain are you? Lights on almost always means somebody is there. So the top of the scale.
3. Result: Somebody must be in.
4. Check what it is not saying. It is not a rule about anybody. Somebody mustn't be in would mean they are forbidden.
Now the other end. You need to find a colleague, and you saw him leave ten minutes ago.
1. How certain are you that he is not in the office? Almost certain.
2. The negative end of the deduction scale is can't, not mustn't.
3. Result: He can't be in the office; I saw him leave.
And the middle. You do not know where somebody is but you have an idea.
1. Possible, not certain: might, may or could — all three work.
2. Result: She might be in the other bay.
grammar.mistake: Using mustn't as the negative of a deduction — he mustn't be in, meaning you think he is not there. That is the obligation use and it says he is forbidden to be there. The other error is omitting be: he must tired, she might in the other bay. The modal is always followed by be or by a plain verb.
grammar.tip: Must, might, can't. The opposite of must be is can't be.
grammar.practice:
Write must, might or can't.
1. The lights are on, so somebody ____ be in.
2. I saw him leave, so he ____ be in the office.
3. She is not answering, so she ____ be in a meeting.
4. It was replaced two weeks ago, so the seal ____ be the cause.
5. He has been working since six, so he ____ be tired.
6. Nobody has told me, so it ____ be urgent, or it ____ not be.
grammar.answers:
1. must  2. can't  3. might (or may, or could)  4. can't  5. must  6. might … might
Numbers 2 and 4 are the negative end of the scale, and both take can't. Neither would be correct with mustn't, which would say they are forbidden.
Numbers 1 and 5 are near-certainty from evidence — lights on, and a long shift.
Number 6 shows that might works in both directions: it might be urgent and it might not be. Can't and must have no such flexibility, because both are near-certain.

grammar.title: Past modals
grammar.explanation: The same scale reaching backwards, plus two forms that only exist in the past — and one confusion that this card exists to fix.
grammar.rule:
ADD HAVE + PAST PARTICIPLE
  must have been     almost certainly was
  might have been    possible
  can't have been    almost certainly not

  "The door was open, so somebody
   must have been in."
  "He can't have seen it; he wasn't there."

TWO THAT ONLY EXIST IN THE PAST
  SHOULD HAVE  the right thing, and it
     did NOT happen
     I should have asked.
     Somebody should have checked it.
  COULD HAVE   possible, and it did NOT
     It could have been much worse.

THE CONFUSION THIS CARD FIXES
  Somebody MUST have checked it.
     = I'm almost certain they DID.
  Somebody SHOULD have checked it.
     = nobody DID, and that was wrong.

  OPPOSITE situations.

THE TEST
  must have -> what DID happen
  should have -> what did NOT

ALSO WORTH HAVING
  needn't have worried
     = I did worry, and it was unnecessary
grammar.workedExample:
You come in and find the door open, which it should not be.
1. Are you deducing what happened, or judging what did not? Deducing.
2. How certain? Doors do not open themselves, so near-certain.
3. Near-certain about the past takes must have plus the participle.
4. Result: Somebody must have been in.
Now the other one. Nobody carried out the weekly check, and they were supposed to.
1. Are you deducing or judging? Judging — you know it did not happen.
2. The right thing that did not happen takes should have.
3. Result: Somebody should have checked it.
4. Apply the test to both. Must have — what did happen. Should have — what did not. Confirmed.
And one at the negative end. Somebody claims a colleague saw the damage, but he was away that week.
1. Near-certain it did not happen: can't have.
2. Result: He can't have seen it; he wasn't there.
grammar.mistake: Using should have where must have belongs, or the reverse. Somebody should have checked it, said when you believe somebody did check it, tells the reader the opposite of what you meant. The other error is of instead of have — should of, must of, could of. It is written that way because it sounds that way, and it is always wrong.
grammar.tip: Must have: what did happen. Should have: what did not.
grammar.practice:
Write must have, might have, can't have, should have or could have.
1. The door was open, so somebody ____ been in.
2. He was away that week, so he ____ seen it.
3. She is not sure, but she ____ forgotten.
4. Nobody checked it, and somebody ____ .
5. It was only a small knock. It ____ been much worse.
6. The log has no entry, so the check ____ been done.
grammar.answers:
1. must have  2. can't have  3. might have  4. should have  5. could have  6. can't have
Numbers 1 and 6 are both deductions and they sit at opposite ends. In 6 the missing log entry is near-conclusive evidence that it was not done.
Number 4 is the judgement form, and notice how it differs from 6: 6 says it did not happen and 4 says it should have. Both are true of the same situation and they are doing different jobs.
Number 5 is could have for something that was possible and did not occur, which is where relief lives rather than regret.

grammar.title: Could and might: options and hedges
grammar.explanation: The second job of could, which has nothing to do with deduction. It puts an idea on the table without pushing it, and it sits on a scale of pressure with should and must.
grammar.rule:
A SECOND JOB FOR COULD
  not a guess about what is true —
  an OPTION.

  We could postpone it.
  You could ask her directly.

THREE AMOUNTS OF PRESSURE
  COULD   an option. No pressure.
  SHOULD  advice. You think it's right.
  MUST    a decision. Not open.

  We could postpone it.
  We should postpone it.
  We must postpone it.
  ^ same structure, very different asks.

WHY COULD IS UNDERVALUED
  it introduces an idea WITHOUT owning it,
  so the other person can consider it
  rather than defend against it.

IT CONNECTS TO UNIT 7
  could and might are HEDGES.
     There might be another way.
     We could try it the other way round.
  Real proposals. Not challenges.

THE CAUTION
  if everything is COULD, nobody knows
  what you think. Keep SHOULD for what
  you recommend.

PAST FORMS - where regret lives
  We could have postponed it. observation
  We should have postponed it. criticism
grammar.workedExample:
You think a meeting should be moved, and you are raising it for the first time with somebody senior.
1. How much pressure do you want to apply? This is a first mention, so none.
2. An option with no pressure takes could: We could postpone it until the inspection is done.
3. Notice what that achieves. They can agree, disagree or ignore it without any of those being a rejection of you.
4. If they do not take it up and you still believe it, escalate on the second exchange: I think we should postpone it. Now it is advice.
5. Must is a decision and belongs only where the matter is genuinely settled.
Now the past. The meeting was not postponed and it went badly.
1. Do you want to observe or to criticise?
2. It could have been postponed is an observation about what was possible.
3. It should have been postponed is a criticism, and combined with the passive from Unit 10 it criticises without naming anybody.
Opening with must, or with should have, leaves you nowhere to go.
grammar.mistake: Opening with should or must where could would do, which asks more of the listener than you intended and makes a first suggestion feel like a demand. The opposite error is the one Unit 7 warns about: hedging everything with could, so that nobody can tell which ideas you actually hold.
grammar.tip: Could is an option, should is advice, must is a decision.
grammar.practice:
Choose could, should or must, and say what changes.
1. First mention of an idea to somebody senior.
2. You genuinely recommend it.
3. The matter is decided and not open to discussion.
4. You want to raise an alternative in a disagreement without making it a contest.
5. It was possible to postpone it and you did not. (past)
6. It was right to postpone it and you did not. (past)
grammar.answers:
1. We could postpone it. — an option, no pressure, easy to decline.
2. We should postpone it. — advice; you are now on record.
3. We must postpone it. — a decision; no discussion invited.
4. We could try it the other way round. — a real proposal that is not a challenge.
5. We could have postponed it. — an observation about what was possible.
6. We should have postponed it. — a criticism, including of yourself.
Numbers 1, 2 and 3 are the same content at three pressures. Nothing is grammatically wrong with any of them; they ask for different things.
Numbers 5 and 6 are the past pair, and the difference is the same: one observes and one judges.
Number 4 is where this card meets Unit 7 — a hedge that raises an alternative without turning the disagreement into a contest.

speaking.title: Speaking 1 — Deduce from evidence
speaking.instructions:
Take twelve situations where you can see evidence but not the answer.
The lights are on. The car is gone. There is no reply. The log is empty.
For each, say a deduction aloud using must, might or can't.
Record all twelve.
Play back and check you never used mustn't. The negative end of deduction is can't, and mustn't is a rule from Level 1 Unit 17.
speaking.tutor: Describe six situations to the tutor and ask it to deduce what has happened in each.

speaking.title: Speaking 2 — Move it backwards
speaking.instructions:
Take the twelve deductions from Speaking 1.
Say each one again in the past, adding have and the participle.
Somebody must be in becomes somebody must have been in.
Record all twelve.
Play back and listen for should of, must of and could of. They are written errors that come from speech, and hearing yourself is the fastest way to catch them.
speaking.tutor: Say six present deductions and ask the tutor to give each one back in the past.

speaking.title: Speaking 3 — Did or did not
speaking.instructions:
Say each pair aloud, five times.
Somebody must have checked it. / Somebody should have checked it.
He must have known. / He should have known.
She must have told them. / She should have told them.
After each pair, say aloud which one means it happened and which means it did not.
Record one full set.
The test is the same every time: must have is about what did happen, should have is about what did not.
speaking.tutor: Say six sentences with must have and should have and ask the tutor whether the thing happened.

speaking.title: Speaking 4 — Three pressures
speaking.instructions:
Take six things you might propose at work or at home.
Say each one three ways: with could, with should, and with must.
After each set, say which you would actually use and why.
Record all eighteen.
Opening with must leaves you nowhere to escalate to. Hearing all three in your own voice makes the difference obvious in a way the card cannot.
speaking.tutor: Propose something to the tutor three ways and ask how much it feels it is being asked to do each time.

speaking.title: Speaking 5 — Deduce a whole situation
speaking.instructions:
Take a real situation where you had to work something out — a fault, a misunderstanding, a delay, something missing.
Speak for two minutes.
State the evidence first, in the past simple.
Then give your deductions, using must have, might have and can't have.
Then say what should have happened and did not.
Record it.
Listen back and check that every must have is supported by something you actually said as evidence.
speaking.tutor: Give the tutor five pieces of evidence and ask it what it deduces, then compare with your own conclusions.

speaking.title: Speaking 6 — Read the conclusions aloud
speaking.instructions:
Open Reading 3.
Read the five pieces of evidence aloud, then the six conclusions.
Then say aloud: which conclusion is the best supported and why.
Then say what makes C5 different from C3, given that both are tentative.
Then say which conclusion states more than its evidence allows, and what it would need to be justified.
Record the last three parts and keep them.
speaking.tutor: Read the tutor the evidence only and ask what it concludes, then compare with the report's conclusions.

writing.title: Writing 1 — Evidence and conclusions
writing.prompt:
Take a real situation you had to work out, or invent one.
Write it in two parts, like Reading 3.
EVIDENCE: five numbered facts, each one checkable, each in the past simple with no modals at all.
CONCLUSIONS: five numbered deductions, each using a modal, each referring to the evidence it rests on.
One conclusion must use must have, one can't have, one might have, one should have, and one must be explicitly marked as speculation with no evidence.
Then write two lines: which conclusion is strongest, and which you were tempted to state more firmly than the evidence allows.
writing.model:
EVIDENCE
E1 The order was placed on 2 February.
E2 The supplier's confirmation email is dated 2 February.
E3 No dispatch notice was received.
E4 The part had still not arrived on 16 February.
E5 When telephoned on 16 February, the supplier said it had been dispatched on the 9th.

CONCLUSIONS
C1 The order can't have been lost at our end, as the supplier confirmed it the same day (E1, E2).
C2 The part must have left the supplier later than the 9th, or not at all — nothing arrived in the following week and no dispatch notice was generated (E3, E4, E5).
C3 The dispatch notice might have failed rather than the dispatch itself, though nothing in E3 distinguishes the two.
C4 Somebody should have chased it when no dispatch notice arrived after three days. Nobody did.
C5 SPECULATION: it is conceivable that the part was dispatched to the old address. There is no evidence for this and the supplier has not been asked.

1. C1 is strongest — two dated documents support it directly and nothing contradicts it.
2. I was tempted to write C2 as the part was never dispatched. The evidence does not support that: it supports either a late dispatch or none, and I cannot yet tell which.
writing.length: Five items of evidence and five conclusions plus two lines
writing.criteria: Five checkable facts with no modals; five conclusions each with a modal and each citing its evidence; one each of must have, can't have, might have and should have; one explicitly marked as speculation; two lines identifying the strongest conclusion and the one you were tempted to overstate
writing.support: Write the evidence first and then refuse to add anything to it while writing the conclusions. Almost every overstated conclusion comes from a fact the writer knows and did not list.
writing.extension: Give somebody only your evidence section and ask what they conclude. Anything they cannot reach was resting on something you did not write down.

writing.title: Writing 2 — Grade the certainty
writing.prompt:
Find a real document that draws conclusions — a report, a news article, a review, an assessment, a recommendation.
Copy out eight sentences that make a claim.
For each, write STATED as fact, DEDUCED, or SPECULATED, and note which modal or hedge signals it.
Then mark any where the strength of the language does not match the strength of the evidence.
Write two lines: how many were properly hedged, and whether any hedge was covering an absence of evidence rather than genuine uncertainty.
writing.model:
1. The unit was moved on 11 March. — STATED. No modal; a dated fact.
2. The damage must have occurred during the move. — DEDUCED. Must have, and it is supported by the dates.
3. Staff may not have been briefed. — DEDUCED, hedged. May not have.
4. It appears that no check was carried out. — DEDUCED. It appears that, which hedges a near-certainty.
5. This is likely to recur. — SPECULATED. Likely to, with no evidence given for a pattern.
6. Management should have identified the risk. — a judgement, not a deduction. Should have.
7. It is possible that the supplier was at fault. — SPECULATED, and no supplier evidence is cited anywhere.
8. The failure was avoidable. — STATED as fact, and it is a judgement stated flatly.

1. Six of the eight were hedged, which is a reasonable proportion for a report of this kind.
2. Number 7 is a hedge covering an absence of evidence rather than genuine uncertainty. It is possible that the supplier was at fault is true of almost anybody, and the sentence adds nothing while appearing to. Number 8 has the opposite problem: it is a judgement with no hedge at all.
writing.length: Eight sentences with verdicts plus two lines
writing.criteria: Eight genuine claims from a real document; each labelled STATED, DEDUCED or SPECULATED with its signal identified; at least one mismatch between language strength and evidence strength identified; two lines including a judgement about whether any hedge covers absent evidence
writing.support: Mark every modal and hedge in the passage before you start classifying. Sentences with none are being stated as fact, whether or not they are facts, and those are often the ones worth questioning.
writing.extension: Rewrite the two worst-calibrated sentences so the language matches the evidence. One will need a hedge added and one will need one removed.

writing.title: Writing 3 — Read the investigation
writing.prompt:
Use the evidence and conclusions in Reading 3. Write full-sentence answers.
1. C1 uses cannot have been. Is that justified by the evidence?
2. C2 uses must have. What exactly does it claim, and which evidence supports it?
3. C3 and C5 are both tentative. Are they equally well supported?
4. C4 uses should have. What kind of claim is that, and how does it differ from the others?
5. C6 says somebody must have known. Is it justified? If not, what would it need?
writing.model:
1. Yes. E1 shows the seal was replaced on 3 March and E2 shows water was found on 17 March, so the original seal cannot have been the cause of damage found two weeks after it was removed. The strongest negative modal is properly earned here.
2. It claims near-certainty about a time window — that the damage occurred between 3 and 17 March. E1 and E2 fix both ends of that window with dates, so the deduction is as strong as the modal.
3. No. C3 rests on E4 and E5 — a move on a date inside the window, and two staff hearing a knock — so may have been damaged is a hedged claim with real support. C5 states plainly that there is no evidence and the supplier has not been contacted, so conceivable is covering an absence of evidence rather than genuine uncertainty. Both are hedged and only one is supported.
4. It is a judgement rather than a deduction. Should have identified says the check did not happen and that it ought to have, which is a statement about what did not occur — where C1, C2 and C3 are all deductions about what did. It is also the only conclusion that assigns fault, and it does so without naming anybody.
5. It is not justified. C6 deduces a state of mind from an event, and nothing in E1 to E5 says who was present during the move, whether anybody looked at the unit afterwards, or whether a knock of that kind would be noticed. It would need evidence that somebody was in a position to know — a witness who saw the unit after the move, or a record that the knock was mentioned at the time.
writing.criteria: Five answers, each a full sentence; answer 2 identifies both the claim and its supporting evidence; answer 3 distinguishes a supported hedge from one covering absent evidence; answer 4 identifies C4 as a judgement rather than a deduction; answer 5 says what specific evidence would be needed
writing.support: Write the five evidence items on one line and then, for each conclusion, list which evidence numbers it cites or implies. Two conclusions cite nothing, and those are the two to examine.
writing.extension: Rewrite C6 so that its language matches its evidence. How much weaker does it become?

writing.title: Writing 4 — Correct the twelve
writing.prompt:
Every sentence has exactly one mistake from this unit.
Write each out correctly and say which pattern it came from.
1. I saw him leave, so he mustn't be in the office.
2. The lights are on, so somebody must in.
3. He must tired — he has been working since six.
4. She might working late.
5. The door was open, so somebody must of been in.
6. He was away that week, so he shouldn't have seen it.
7. Somebody should have checked it. (you are certain somebody did)
8. Somebody must have checked it. (nobody did, and that was wrong)
9. I needn't have worried. (you never worried at all)
10. We must postpone it. (you are raising the idea for the first time)
11. It should have been much worse. (it was possible and it did not happen)
12. Somebody must have known. (there is no evidence anybody was in a position to know)
writing.model:
1. He can't be in the office. (Pattern 1 — the negative of deduction is can't, not mustn't)
2. Somebody must be in. (Pattern 1 — the modal needs be)
3. He must be tired. (Pattern 1 — same rule)
4. She might be working late. (Pattern 1 — an action in progress takes be plus -ing)
5. Somebody must have been in. (Pattern 2 — have, not of; the error comes from how it sounds)
6. He can't have seen it. (Pattern 2 — near-certainty that it did not happen takes can't have)
7. Somebody must have checked it. (Pattern 2 — certainty that it did happen)
8. Somebody should have checked it. (Pattern 2 — it did not happen and that was wrong)
9. I didn't need to worry. (Pattern 2 — needn't have means you did worry unnecessarily)
10. We could postpone it. (Pattern 3 — a first suggestion takes could, not must)
11. It could have been much worse. (Pattern 3 — possible and did not happen)
12. Somebody may have known. (Pattern 2 — the modal must match the evidence, and there is none)
writing.criteria: All twelve corrected; each labelled with the right pattern; numbers 7 and 8 corrected in opposite directions; number 12 corrected by weakening the modal rather than changing the content
writing.support: Numbers 7 and 8 are the central confusion of the unit, swapped. Apply the test to both before changing either: must have is about what did happen, should have is about what did not.
writing.extension: Number 12 was grammatically perfect and overstated its evidence. Write two more like it.

activities.title: Practice 1 — Deduce
activities.instructions:
Write must, might or can't.
1. The lights are on, so somebody ____ be in.
2. I saw him leave, so he ____ be in the office.
3. She is not answering, so she ____ be in a meeting.
4. The seal was replaced two weeks ago, so it ____ be the cause.
5. He has been working since six, so he ____ be tired.
6. Nobody has told me, so it ____ be urgent — or it ____ not be.
7. The log is empty, so the check ____ have been recorded.
8. Her coat is here, so she ____ be in the building.
9. There is no reply, so she ____ be away, but I am not sure.
10. It is only ten degrees, so the heating ____ be working.
11. He was in another country, so he ____ have been there.
12. The order was confirmed the same day, so it ____ have been lost here.
activities.answers:
1. must  2. can't  3. might  4. can't  5. must  6. might … might  7. can't  8. must  9. might  10. can't  11. can't  12. can't
Five of the twelve are can't, and every one is near-certainty that something is not the case. None of them would be correct with mustn't, which would say the thing is forbidden.
Numbers 1, 5 and 8 are near-certainty in the positive direction, each resting on a piece of visible evidence.
Number 6 shows might working in both directions at once. Must and can't cannot do that, because both are near-certain.
Numbers 7, 11 and 12 are past deductions, and the negative is still can't have rather than mustn't have.

activities.title: Practice 2 — Must have or should have?
activities.instructions:
Write must have, might have, can't have, should have or could have, and mark DID or DID NOT for whether the thing happened.
1. The door was open, so somebody ____ been in.
2. He was away, so he ____ seen it.
3. She is not sure, but she ____ forgotten.
4. Nobody checked it, and somebody ____ .
5. It was only a small knock. It ____ been much worse.
6. The log has no entry, so the check ____ been done.
7. The confirmation is dated the same day, so they ____ received it.
8. Nobody told the warehouse, and somebody ____ .
9. She may not be certain, but she ____ mentioned it.
10. He had already left, so he ____ heard the announcement.
11. The fault was obvious, so somebody ____ noticed it.
12. It was avoidable. We ____ postponed it.
13. The supplier confirmed it, so it ____ been lost here.
14. Nobody raised it, and somebody ____ .
15. He was in the room, so he ____ heard it.
16. The risk was foreseeable, so it ____ been anticipated.
activities.answers:
1. must have — DID  2. can't have — DID NOT  3. might have — possibly  4. should have — DID NOT  5. could have — DID NOT  6. can't have — DID NOT  7. must have — DID  8. should have — DID NOT  9. might have — possibly  10. can't have — DID NOT  11. must have — DID  12. should have — DID NOT  13. can't have — DID NOT  14. should have — DID NOT  15. must have — DID  16. should have — DID NOT
The must have items — 1, 7, 11, 15 — all say the thing happened, and each rests on evidence that makes it near-certain.
The should have items — 4, 8, 12, 14, 16 — all say the thing did not happen and that it ought to have. Notice that every one of them assigns a failure without naming anybody.
Number 11 is worth a second look. Must have noticed is a deduction about a state of mind, and it is much weaker than a deduction about an event — which is exactly the problem with C6 in Reading 3.

activities.title: Practice 3 — Three pressures
activities.instructions:
Write the same proposal three ways — with could, should and must — then say which you would use in the situation described.
1. Postponing a meeting. (first mention, to somebody senior)
2. Replacing a supplier. (you genuinely recommend it)
3. Stopping work on a bay. (a safety issue, already decided)
4. Asking somebody directly. (raising it in a disagreement)
5. Checking the figures again. (you think it is worth doing)
6. Reporting it today. (a deadline makes it non-negotiable)
activities.answers:
1. We could postpone it. / We should postpone it. / We must postpone it. — use could; a first mention to somebody senior should be declinable.
2. We could change supplier. / We should change supplier. / We must change supplier. — use should; you are recommending, and should puts you on record.
3. We could stop work on that bay. / We should stop. / We must stop. — use must; a decided safety issue is not an option.
4. You could ask her directly. / You should ask her. / You must ask her. — use could; in a disagreement it raises the alternative without making it a contest.
5. We could check them again. / We should check them again. / We must check them. — use should; you think it is worth doing, which is advice.
6. We could report it today. / We should report it today. / We must report it today. — use must; a deadline removes the choice.
Three of the six take could or should, and only two genuinely take must. That ratio is normal — must is for the things that are actually settled, and using it earlier spends its force.
In every set, nothing is grammatically wrong with any of the three. What changes is how much you are asking of the person you are speaking to.

activities.title: Practice 4 — Match the modal to the evidence
activities.instructions:
For each conclusion, write JUSTIFIED or OVERSTATED given the evidence in brackets. Rewrite the overstated ones.
1. The seal can't have been the cause. (it was replaced two weeks before the damage was found)
2. The damage must have occurred in the two-week window. (both dates are documented)
3. The unit may have been damaged during the move. (two staff heard a knock; nobody saw the unit afterwards)
4. The replacement seal must have been faulty. (no evidence; the supplier has not been contacted)
5. Somebody must have known. (nothing about who was present or what was noticed)
6. The check can't have been done. (the log has no entry for that period)
7. It will happen again. (one occurrence)
8. Staff may not have been briefed. (no briefing record exists)
activities.answers:
1. JUSTIFIED.
2. JUSTIFIED.
3. JUSTIFIED — may have is appropriately hedged for a knock that nobody connected to the unit.
4. OVERSTATED. Rewrite: it is conceivable that the replacement seal was faulty, though there is no evidence and the supplier has not been contacted.
5. OVERSTATED. Rewrite: somebody may have known, though nothing establishes who was in a position to notice.
6. JUSTIFIED — a missing log entry is near-conclusive for a check that is required to be logged.
7. OVERSTATED. Rewrite: it could happen again, and nothing has been changed to prevent it.
8. JUSTIFIED — may not have is correctly hedged, and the absent record supports it.
The three overstated items all have the same shape: the strength of the modal does not match the strength of the evidence.
Numbers 4 and 5 are the important pair. In 4 the hedge is missing; in 5 the deduction is about a state of mind, which is always weaker than a deduction about an event.
Number 6 is worth noticing as a contrast with 5: a missing record is evidence of absence, because the record was required. A missing mention is not.

activities.title: Practice 5 — Deduce from a real situation
activities.instructions:
This week, take one real situation you had to work out — something missing, a delay, a misunderstanding, a fault.
Write the evidence as five numbered facts, with no modals at all.
Then write your conclusions with modals, each citing its evidence.
Then give somebody only the evidence and ask what they conclude.
Write two lines on where their conclusions differed from yours and why.
activities.answers:
No key — it is your situation.
What most people find: separating evidence from conclusion is much harder than it looks, and the first draft of the evidence section usually contains at least one conclusion disguised as a fact. Nobody checked it is a conclusion; the log has no entry is a fact.
The second finding is about the other person. They will nearly always reach fewer conclusions than you did, and the gap is the knowledge you have that never made it onto the page. That is the same finding as in Writing 1's extension, and it is the most useful thing this task produces.
Occasionally they reach a conclusion you did not, and that is worth more attention still — it usually means you had ruled something out on evidence you forgot you had.

activities.title: Practice 6 — Listen for the hedges
activities.instructions:
This week, listen for deduction in real speech or reading — somebody working out what happened.
Write down six examples exactly.
For each, note the modal used and whether the speaker was reasoning or reporting.
Then note how many used mustn't for a negative deduction. It should be none.
activities.answers:
No key.
What most people find: deduction is everywhere once you listen for it. Must be and might be do most of the work in speech, and can't be appears whenever somebody is ruling something out.
The second finding is the one to confirm for yourself: mustn't never appears as a negative deduction in fluent English. If you hear it, it is about a rule. That confirms the card's central point from real data rather than from assertion.
The third finding is about hedging. Speakers hedge deductions far more than they hedge reports of what they saw, and they do it without thinking about it. I saw him leave is flat; he must have gone home is hedged, even though the speaker is fairly sure. That difference is the natural register for reasoning, and copying it will make your own deductions sound considerably more careful.

quizzes.q: The lights are on. Which is correct?
quizzes.why: This is deduction, not a rule. The modal is followed by be, and mustn't would mean somebody is forbidden to be there.

quizzes.q: You saw him leave. What is the opposite of he must be in?
quizzes.why: Obligation negates with mustn't; deduction negates with can't. This is the point that catches almost everybody.

quizzes.q: Which is correct for something in progress?
quizzes.why: For an action in progress the modal takes be plus the -ing form, exactly as the continuous does elsewhere.

quizzes.q: Somebody must have checked it. What does this mean?
options: I am almost certain somebody did check it
Nobody checked it and that was wrong
Somebody was required to check it
quizzes.a: I am almost certain somebody did check it
quizzes.why: Must have is a deduction about what did happen. Should have would mean the opposite — that nobody did, and that it was wrong.

quizzes.q: Somebody should have checked it. What does this mean?
options: Nobody checked it, and that was wrong
quizzes.a: Nobody checked it, and that was wrong
quizzes.why: Should have is a judgement about what did not happen. It is also how English assigns a failure without naming anybody.

quizzes.q: What is the test that separates must have from should have?
options: Must have is formal; should have is informal
Must have is past; should have is present
Must have is about what did happen; should have is about what did not
quizzes.a: Must have is about what did happen; should have is about what did not
quizzes.why: They describe opposite situations, and the test resolves any sentence in one step.
Must of is a written error that comes from how must have sounds in speech. It is always wrong.

quizzes.q: I needn't have worried. What does this mean?
options: I worried, and it turned out to be unnecessary
quizzes.a: I worried, and it turned out to be unnecessary
quizzes.why: I didn't need to worry is the different one — it means it was unnecessary and you may never have worried at all.

quizzes.q: You are raising an idea for the first time with somebody senior. Which fits?
quizzes.why: Could is an option with no pressure, so they can consider it rather than defend against it. Opening with must leaves you nowhere to escalate to.

quizzes.q: What is the scale of pressure?
quizzes.why: Could is an option, should is advice, and must is a decision. Choosing wrongly is not a grammar error and it changes how much you are asking.

quizzes.q: Conclusion C5 says it is conceivable, with no evidence cited. What is the hedge doing?
options: Covering an absence of evidence rather than genuine uncertainty
quizzes.a: Covering an absence of evidence rather than genuine uncertainty
quizzes.why: C3 is also hedged and rests on two pieces of evidence. Being hedged and being supported are different things.

quizzes.q: C6 says somebody must have known. Why is it weaker than C2?
options: It deduces a state of mind rather than an event, with no supporting evidence
It appears later in the report
quizzes.a: It deduces a state of mind rather than an event, with no supporting evidence
quizzes.why: C2 fixes a time window from two dated facts. C6 has nothing about who was present or what anybody noticed, and states it just as strongly.

teacherNotes.note: Three pattern cards, each with a worked example, and every exercise has an answer key or an explicit no-key note with a what-most-people-find finding. Practice 2 is the diagnostic and it asks for DID or DID NOT alongside every answer, because the must have and should have confusion is about what occurred rather than about the form.

teacherNotes.type: This unit was rescoped and the plan was corrected
teacherNotes.note: The plan originally titled it Certainty, Obligation and Possibility and included strong and weak obligation, which Level 1 Units 11 and 17 already own. The obligation pattern was removed during the level audit and the title has been changed to match. If a learner asks why must appears in two levels doing different jobs, that is the answer, and Reading 1 states it directly.

teacherNotes.type: The negative is where the two jobs separate
teacherNotes.note: Obligation negates with mustn't and deduction negates with can't, and learners produce he mustn't be in constantly. Practice 1 loads five can't items for this reason, and Practice 6 asks learners to confirm from real speech that mustn't never appears as a negative deduction. That confirmation from data is more convincing than the rule.

teacherNotes.type: Must have versus should have is the central confusion
teacherNotes.note: They describe opposite situations — one says the thing happened, the other says it did not — and learners use them interchangeably well into B2. The test is one line and resolves everything. Writing 4 numbers 7 and 8 are the pair swapped, and Speaking 3 drills three pairs aloud with the learner stating which happened after each.

Could has a second job that is nothing to do with certainty, and the could-should-must scale of pressure is the same register work as the opinion frames in Unit 7. Practice 3 gives six situations and only two genuinely take must, which is the ratio worth showing — must spends its force if used early.

Every conclusion in it is a deduction, so the modals carry the entire epistemic content. Four of the six are properly calibrated, one hedges an absence of evidence rather than genuine uncertainty, and one deduces a state of mind from an event with nothing supporting it. Distinguishing a supported hedge from an unsupported one is the hardest comprehension in the unit and it is what Writing 2 then asks learners to do on a real document.

The AI tutor is a rehearsal partner and no task here is scored by it alone. Speaking 5, Writing 1 and Practice 5 ask learners to reason about a real situation, which may involve a workplace incident, a dispute or somebody else's conduct: no names, employers or identifying details should be collected, shared or entered into the app, and learners may invent the situation instead. Writing 2 sends learners to a real document, and no sentence from one about their own circumstances should be entered either. Practice 5 asks another person only what they conclude from the evidence, not for any judgement about the people involved.

selfAssessment.statement: I can say he must be in and he can't be in, and know neither is about rules.
I can tell the difference between somebody must have checked it and somebody should have checked it.
I can say we could, we should and we must and mean three different amounts of pressure.
I can read a conclusion and tell how certain the writer actually is.

assignment.title: A situation deduced, and a report graded
assignment.instructions: Two parts. First, record two minutes reasoning from evidence to conclusions about something you had to work out — stating the evidence first in the past simple, then the deductions with must have, might have and can't have, then what should have happened and did not; then record the six could, should and must sets from Speaking 4 saying which you would actually use each time. Second, write the evidence-and-conclusions document from Writing 1 with its two lines of commentary, grade eight claims from a real document as directed in Writing 2, and add your full-sentence answers to the five questions in Writing 3. Keep everything together.
assignment.submissionType: An audio recording and written work
